claim: The white-eye genus Zosterops comprises approximately 100 species from across the Old World.
source: The white-eye genus Zosterops is a classical example of a 'great speciator', comprising c. 100 species from across the Old World, most of them insular.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the taxonomic framework used in the study.

claim: Most Zosterops species are insular.
source: The white-eye genus Zosterops is a classical example of a 'great speciator', comprising c. 100 species from across the Old World, most of them insular.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the distribution data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The Zosterops phylogeny comprises three main clades centered in Indo-Africa, Asia, and Australasia.
source: Using over 700 genome-wide loci in conjunction with coalescent species tree methods and gene flow detection approaches, we untangled the reticulated evolutionary history of Zosterops, which comprises three main clades centered in Indo-Africa, Asia, and Australasia, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by phylogenetic analyses using multiple methods (MP-EST, STAR, ASTRID) and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Genetic introgression between species permeates the Zosterops phylogeny, regardless of how distantly related species are.
source: Genetic introgression between species permeates the Zosterops phylogeny, regardless of how distantly related species are.
evidence: This is supported by ABBA-BABA test results shown in Table 1 and PHRAPL analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Indonesian archipelago is the major center of diversity for Zosterops where all three main clades overlap.
source: Crucially, we identified the Indonesian archipelago, and specifically Borneo, as the major center of diversity and the only area where all three main clades overlap, attesting to the evolutionary importance of this region.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic distribution data shown in Figure 2a and discussed in the results section.

claim: Borneo is the only area where all three main Zosterops clades overlap.
source: Crucially, we identified the Indonesian archipelago, and specifically Borneo, as the major center of diversity and the only area where all three main clades overlap, attesting to the evolutionary importance of this region.
evidence: This is supported by the distribution data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Zosterops is one of the few classical examples of 'great speciators' identified by Diamond et al., 1976.
source: One of the few classical examples of 'great speciators' identified by Diamond et al., 1976 is the songbird genus Zosterops, or white-eyes, which are dispersers capable of differentiating rapidly from source populations (Clegg et al., 2002; Moyle et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Diamond et al., 1976 and subsequent studies.

claim: Zosterops radiated across the Old World and Oceania within the past 1–3.5 million years.
source: The genus Zosterops comprises c. 100 species that have radiated across the Old World and Oceania within the past 1–3.5 million years, reflecting one of the fastest diversification rates among vertebrates (Warren et al., 2006; Moyle et al., 2009; Jetz et al., 2012; Leroy et al., 2019; Cai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies on Zosterops diversification timing.

claim: Zosterops reflects one of the fastest diversification rates among vertebrates.
source: The genus Zosterops comprises c. 100 species that have radiated across the Old World and Oceania within the past 1–3.5 million years, reflecting one of the fastest diversification rates among vertebrates (Warren et al., 2006; Moyle et al., 2009; Jetz et al., 2012; Leroy et al., 2019; Cai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on vertebrate diversification rates.

claim: More than 70% of Zosterops species occur exclusively in archipelagoes distributed across the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.
source: An overwhelming proportion (more than 70%) of these species occurs exclusively in archipelagoes distributed across the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the distribution map in Figure 1.

claim: The Indonesian archipelago comprises more than 17,000 islands.
source: In particular, it is crucial to unravel the phylogenetic affinities of white-eyes distributed across the Indonesian archipelago, which – comprising more than 17,000 islands – is the largest archipelago in the world and harbors about 20 endemic Zosterops species (Figure 1), including two species that were discovered in the last two decades and remain undescribed (Eaton et al., 2016; O'Connell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Indonesian archipelago supported by general geographic knowledge.

claim: The Indonesian archipelago is the largest archipelago in the world.
source: In particular, it is crucial to unravel the phylogenetic affinities of white-eyes distributed across the Indonesian archipelago, which – comprising more than 17,000 islands – is the largest archipelago in the world and harbors about 20 endemic Zosterops species (Figure 1), including two species that were discovered in the last two decades and remain undescribed (Eaton et al., 2016; O'Connell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a factual statement supported by general geographic knowledge.

claim: The Indonesian archipelago harbors about 20 endemic Zosterops species.
source: In particular, it is crucial to unravel the phylogenetic affinities of white-eyes distributed across the Indonesian archipelago, which – comprising more than 17,000 islands – is the largest archipelago in the world and harbors about 20 endemic Zosterops species (Figure 1), including two species that were discovered in the last two decades and remain undescribed (Eaton et al., 2016; O'Connell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the distribution data in Figure 1.

claim: Two Zosterops species discovered in the Indonesian archipelago in the last two decades remain undescribed.
source: In particular, it is crucial to unravel the phylogenetic affinities of white-eyes distributed across the Indonesian archipelago, which – comprising more than 17,000 islands – is the largest archipelago in the world and harbors about 20 endemic Zosterops species (Figure 1), including two species that were discovered in the last two decades and remain undescribed (Eaton et al., 2016; O'Connell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eaton et al., 2016 and O'Connell et al., 2019.

claim: Most phylogenetic studies of white-eyes have been restricted to one or a few genetic markers.
source: Apart from incomplete geographic sampling, the lack of resolution of the white-eye radiation has largely been a consequence of sparse genomic sampling: most phylogenetic studies of white-eyes have been restricted to one or a few genetic markers, resulting in trees that are plagued by unresolved polytomies, hampering useful evolutionary inference (Slikas et al., 2000; Warren et al., 2006; Moyle et al., 2009; Oatley et al., 2012; Á.S and Joseph, 2013; Cox et al., 2014; Husemann et al., 2016; Linck et al., 2016; Round et al., 2017; Wickramasinghe et al., 2017; Shakya et al., 2018; Cai et al., 2019; Lim et al., 2019; O'Connell et al., 2019; Martins et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to numerous previous phylogenetic studies of Zosterops.

claim: Previous phylogenetic studies of white-eyes resulted in trees plagued by unresolved polytomies.
source: Apart from incomplete geographic sampling, the lack of resolution of the white-eye radiation has largely been a consequence of sparse genomic sampling: most phylogenetic studies of white-eyes have been restricted to one or a few genetic markers, resulting in trees that are plagued by unresolved polytomies, hampering useful evolutionary inference (Slikas et al., 2000; Warren et al., 2006; Moyle et al., 2009; Oatley et al., 2012; Á.S and Joseph, 2013; Cox et al., 2014; Husemann et al., 2016; Linck et al., 2016; Round et al., 2017; Wickramasinghe et al., 2017; Shakya et al., 2018; Cai et al., 2019; Lim et al., 2019; O'Connell et al., 2019; Martins et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies and by the mitochondrial tree shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The multispecies coalescent model offers a promising avenue to overcoming gene tree discordance.
source: The multispecies coalescent (MSC) model offers a promising avenue to overcoming gene tree discordance by allowing the evolutionary histories of each locus to be inferred independently (Song et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological papers on the MSC model.

claim: The study used over 700 genome-wide loci for phylogenetic analysis.
source: Using more than 700 genome-wide loci with a dense species sampling, our study produced an improved phylogeny of Zosterops and reveals the existence of three discrete main clades characterized by an Indo-African, Asiatic, and Australasian core of distribution, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the methods section describing 770 loci used in analyses.

claim: The study sampled 33 white-eye species.
source: Our taxon sampling covered 33 out of 108 white-eye species across the global radiation (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The study used historical specimens and recently collected samples.
source: In this study, we used historical specimens and recently collected samples to represent 33 white-eye species across the Southern hemisphere, especially from the understudied Indonesian archipelago (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and detailed in the methods section.

claim: RNA probes were designed using Z. lateralis as a reference genome.
source: We designed RNA probes using Z. lateralis (Cornetti et al., 2015) as a reference genome, targeting 832 loci at high coverage to overcome the limitations of missing data expected from degraded DNA of historical samples, thereby recovering a comparable set of loci across both historical and fresh samples (Templeton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and detailed in the methods section.

claim: The study targeted 832 loci at high coverage.
source: We designed RNA probes using Z. lateralis (Cornetti et al., 2015) as a reference genome, targeting 832 loci at high coverage to overcome the limitations of missing data expected from degraded DNA of historical samples, thereby recovering a comparable set of loci across both historical and fresh samples (Templeton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and detailed in the methods section.

claim: Three different coalescent species tree methods were employed: MP-EST, STAR, and ASTRID.
source: We employed three different coalescent species tree methods to assess topological incongruence across tree-building approaches (Liu et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010; Vachaspati and Warnow, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and detailed in the methods section.

claim: All four tree inference methods produced a similar phylogeny with congruent tree topology for highly supported nodes.
source: All four tree inference methods produced a similar phylogeny with a congruent tree topology for highly supported nodes, except for the placement of a Sundaic group consisting of Z. atricapilla and Z. auriventer (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The placement of Z. atricapilla and Z. auriventer differs between concatenated and species trees.
source: All four tree inference methods produced a similar phylogeny with a congruent tree topology for highly supported nodes, except for the placement of a Sundaic group consisting of Z. atricapilla and Z. auriventer (Figure 2). These two Sundaic taxa are embedded within the Australasian clade in the concatenated tree, but emerged within the Asiatic clade in the species trees constructed with MP-EST (henceforth our baseline species tree) and ASTRID (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Z. atricapilla and Z. auriventer are embedded within the Australasian clade in the concatenated tree.
source: These two Sundaic taxa are embedded within the Australasian clade in the concatenated tree, but emerged within the Asiatic clade in the species trees constructed with MP-EST (henceforth our baseline species tree) and ASTRID (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Z. atricapilla and Z. auriventer emerged within the Asiatic clade in the MP-EST and ASTRID species trees.
source: These two Sundaic taxa are embedded within the Australasian clade in the concatenated tree, but emerged within the Asiatic clade in the species trees constructed with MP-EST (henceforth our baseline species tree) and ASTRID (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: STAR shows weak bootstrap support for an unresolved placement of Z. atricapilla and Z. auriventer.
source: The other species tree method, STAR, shows a weak bootstrap support for an unresolved placement of these Sundaic taxa.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The Afrotropical region harbors only members of the Indo-African clade.
source: Therefore, our mapping suggests that the Afrotropical and the Australo-Papuan regions are depauperate in deeper Zosterops lineage diversity (Figure 2a; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The Australo-Papuan region is depauperate in deeper Zosterops lineage diversity.
source: Therefore, our mapping suggests that the Afrotropical and the Australo-Papuan regions are depauperate in deeper Zosterops lineage diversity (Figure 2a; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Most areas in continental Asia harbor only one of the three main Zosterops clades.
source: Similarly, our results reveal that most areas in continental Asia generally harbor only one of the three main Zosterops clades, except East Asia where two clades co-occur in a narrow zone of overlap between the Indo-African Z. palpebrosus and the Asiatic Z. simplex (orange in Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: In East Asia, two Zosterops clades co-occur in a narrow zone of overlap between Z. palpebrosus and Z. simplex.
source: Similarly, our results reveal that most areas in continental Asia generally harbor only one of the three main Zosterops clades, except East Asia where two clades co-occur in a narrow zone of overlap between the Indo-African Z. palpebrosus and the Asiatic Z. simplex (orange in Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: All three main Zosterops clades are represented on Java and Borneo.
source: In contrast, the Indonesian archipelago emerged as a center of modern-day diversity for Zosterops, with all three main clades represented on Java and Borneo, and two main clades on many other islands (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Two main Zosterops clades occur on many Indonesian islands other than Java and Borneo.
source: In contrast, the Indonesian archipelago emerged as a center of modern-day diversity for Zosterops, with all three main clades represented on Java and Borneo, and two main clades on many other islands (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: PHRAPL simulations show that Z. auriventer is more closely related to Z. simplex than to Z. emiliae.
source: The top two demographic models inferred by PHRAPL simulations show that Sundaic Z. auriventer is more closely related to Asiatic Z. simplex than to Australasian Z. emiliae, but inconclusive in relation to Z. melanurus due to ancestral and/or secondary gene flow between all three taxa (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: PHRAPL results are inconclusive regarding the relationship of Z. auriventer to Z. melanurus due to gene flow.
source: The top two demographic models inferred by PHRAPL simulations show that Sundaic Z. auriventer is more closely related to Asiatic Z. simplex than to Australasian Z. emiliae, but inconclusive in relation to Z. melanurus due to ancestral and/or secondary gene flow between all three taxa (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Ancestral and/or secondary gene flow was detected between Z. atricapilla, Z. simplex, and Z. emiliae.
source: Additionally, ancestral and/or secondary gene flow was detected between all taxa in both comparisons involving Z. atricapilla, Z. simplex, and either Z. emiliae or Z. melanurus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The genealogical divergence index (gdi) of the top demographic model for each combination ranges between 0.321 and 0.751.
source: The genealogical divergence index (gdi) of the top demographic model inferred for each combination is relatively high, ranging between 0.321 and 0.751, suggesting high divergence between sister species despite secondary gene flow.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: High gdi values suggest high divergence between sister species despite secondary gene flow.
source: The genealogical divergence index (gdi) of the top demographic model inferred for each combination is relatively high, ranging between 0.321 and 0.751, suggesting high divergence between sister species despite secondary gene flow.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gdi values based on the definition of the index.

claim: ABBA-BABA statistics revealed a significant excess of allele sharing between the Sundaic taxa and Z. melanurus and Z. citrinella.
source: The ABBA-BABA statistics revealed a significant excess of allele sharing between the Sundaic taxa (Z. atricapilla and Z. auriventer) and two Australasian taxa (Z. melanurus and Z. citrinella) (Figure 3c, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3c and Table 1.

claim: Ancestral introgression occurred between the Sundaic taxa and the Australasian lineage after Z. emiliae had diverged.
source: This result reflects that ancestral introgression occurred between the Sundaic taxa and the Australasian lineage after Z. emiliae had diverged (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ABBA-BABA results shown in Figure 3c and Table 1.

claim: Secondary gene flow was detected between Z. auriventer and Z. simplex.
source: In addition, secondary gene flow was also detected in several pairs of species which overlap in present-day distribution (sets 2 to 4 in Table 1). For instance, we found that Z. melanurus shares significantly more alleles with Z. simplex than with Z. erythropleurus, suggesting occasional hybridization between Z. melanurus buxtoni and Z. simplex erwini on Sumatra, where both occur. In a similar vein, Z. erythropleurus and Z. japonicus displayed excess allele sharing, indicating potential introgression in areas of overlap in Korea, and Z. auriventer and Z. simplex exhibited excess allele sharing that hints at occasional hybridization in parts of peninsular Malaysia and Borneo where they overlap.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: Z. melanurus shares significantly more alleles with Z. simplex than with Z. erythropleurus.
source: For instance, we found that Z. melanurus shares significantly more alleles with Z. simplex than with Z. erythropleurus, suggesting occasional hybridization between Z. melanurus buxtoni and Z. simplex erwini on Sumatra, where both occur.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: Occasional hybridization occurs between Z. melanurus buxtoni and Z. simplex erwini on Sumatra.
source: For instance, we found that Z. melanurus shares significantly more alleles with Z. simplex than with Z. erythropleurus, suggesting occasional hybridization between Z. melanurus buxtoni and Z. simplex erwini on Sumatra, where both occur.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ABBA-BABA results shown in Table 1.

claim: Z. erythropleurus and Z. japonicus displayed excess allele sharing.
source: In a similar vein, Z. erythropleurus and Z. japonicus displayed excess allele sharing, indicating potential introgression in areas of overlap in Korea, and Z. auriventer and Z. simplex exhibited excess allele sharing that hints at occasional hybridization in parts of peninsular Malaysia and Borneo where they overlap.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: Potential introgression occurs between Z. erythropleurus and Z. japonicus in areas of overlap in Korea.
source: In a similar vein, Z. erythropleurus and Z. japonicus displayed excess allele sharing, indicating potential introgression in areas of overlap in Korea, and Z. auriventer and Z. simplex exhibited excess allele sharing that hints at occasional hybridization in parts of peninsular Malaysia and Borneo where they overlap.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ABBA-BABA results shown in Table 1.

claim: Occasional hybridization occurs between Z. auriventer and Z. simplex in parts of peninsular Malaysia and Borneo.
source: In a similar vein, Z. erythropleurus and Z. japonicus displayed excess allele sharing, indicating potential introgression in areas of overlap in Korea, and Z. auriventer and Z. simplex exhibited excess allele sharing that hints at occasional hybridization in parts of peninsular Malaysia and Borneo where they overlap.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ABBA-BABA results shown in Table 1.

claim: The evolutionary history of Zosterops has received scientific attention mostly by means of single mitochondrial or few nuclear loci.
source: The evolutionary history of Zosterops has received a fair amount of scientific attention, but mostly by means of single mitochondrial or few nuclear loci, therefore resulting in trees plagued by unresolved polytomies (e.g. Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Degnan and Moritz, 1992; Degnan, 1993; Slikas et al., 2000; Warren et al., 2006; Moyle et al., 2009; Oatley et al., 2012; Á.S and Joseph, 2013; Cox et al., 2014; Husemann et al., 2016; Linck et al., 2016; Round et al., 2017; Wickramasinghe et al., 2017; Shakya et al., 2018; Cai et al., 2019; Lim et al., 2019; O'Connell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to numerous previous studies.

claim: There was no strong support to unravel the sequence of diversification events among the three main Zosterops clades.
source: However, there was no strong support to unravel the sequence of diversification events among those three main clades.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: Lack of basal resolution could be attributed to a quick succession of divergence events and/or reticulated evolutionary history.
source: This lack of basal resolution could be attributed to a quick succession of divergence events at the time, and/or reticulated evolutionary history unresolved by species tree and concatenated tree approaches.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the lack of resolution.

claim: Uncertainties in the affinity of Z. atricapilla and Z. auriventer appear to be due to secondary gene flow between the incipient Asiatic and Australasian clades.
source: Uncertainties in the affinity of these two Sundaic species appear to be due to secondary gene flow between the incipient Asiatic and Australasian clades (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PHRAPL and ABBA-BABA results shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Genetic introgression destabilizes the robustness of the MSC model.
source: Such genetic introgression destabilizes the robustness of the MSC model, which does not account for secondary gene flow, thereby confounding species tree estimation (Figure 3, Table 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the MSC model supported by methodological knowledge.

claim: Traditional phylogenetic approaches such as concatenation are negatively impacted by secondary gene flow and incomplete lineage sorting.
source: At the same time, traditional phylogenetic approaches such as concatenation are equally negatively impacted by secondary gene flow and are additionally subject to the biases of incomplete lineage sorting (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Most of the top demographic models inferred by PHRAPL produced topologies in which the Sundaic species emerge as sister to the Asiatic clade.
source: Most of the top demographic models inferred by PHRAPL produced topologies in which the Sundaic species of controversial placement emerge as sister to the Asiatic clade (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The detection of rampant secondary gene flow in multiple pairs of sympatric white-eye species is in agreement with recent discovery of introgression between various non-sister white-eye species across the Solomon Islands.
source: The detection of rampant secondary gene flow in multiple pairs of sympatric white-eye species is in agreement with the recent discovery of introgression between various non-sister white-eye species across the Solomon Islands (Manthey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manthey et al., 2020.

claim: Africa harbors representatives from only one of the three main Zosterops clades.
source: Our phylogenetic results demonstrate that Africa, most parts of continental Asia and probably also all of the Australo-Papuan region each harbor representatives from only one of the three main Zosterops clades, respectively (Figure 2a), regardless of Zosterops species diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Most parts of continental Asia harbor representatives from only one of the three main Zosterops clades.
source: Our phylogenetic results demonstrate that Africa, most parts of continental Asia and probably also all of the Australo-Papuan region each harbor representatives from only one of the three main Zosterops clades, respectively (Figure 2a), regardless of Zosterops species diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Probably all of the Australo-Papuan region harbors representatives from only one of the three main Zosterops clades.
source: Our phylogenetic results demonstrate that Africa, most parts of continental Asia and probably also all of the Australo-Papuan region each harbor representatives from only one of the three main Zosterops clades, respectively (Figure 2a), regardless of Zosterops species diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with qualification ('probably') and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Virtually all parts of the Indonesian archipelago harbor white-eye species from two to three of the main Zosterops clades.
source: In contrast, virtually all parts of the Indonesian archipelago harbor white-eye species from two to three of the main Zosterops clades (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The Indonesian islands are a center of syntopy of lineages from either side of Wallace's Line.
source: Positioned between the Sunda and Sahul shelf, the Indonesian islands are a center of syntopy of lineages from either side of Wallace's Line (Moss and Wilson, 1998; de Bruyn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moss and Wilson, 1998 and de Bruyn et al., 2014.

claim: Rapid tectonic change has been reconstructed for the Indonesian archipelago over the last 30 million years.
source: This is consistent with the rapid rate of tectonic change reconstructed for the Indonesian archipelago over the last 30 million years (Hall, 2002; Hall, 2012; de Bruyn et al., 2014; Nugraha and Hall, 2018), which has led to a narrowing of open sea between Asia and Australia and thereby facilitated overwater dispersal of Sundaic and/or Australo-Papuan lineages for many organismic groups (e.g. Heads, 2001; Irestedt et al., 2013; Gwee et al., 2017; Ng et al., 2017; Garg et al., 2018; Reilly et al., 2019; Oliver et al., 2020, including white-eyes).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple geological studies.

claim: Tectonic change has led to a narrowing of open sea between Asia and Australia.
source: This is consistent with the rapid rate of tectonic change reconstructed for the Indonesian archipelago over the last 30 million years (Hall, 2002; Hall, 2012; de Bruyn et al., 2014; Nugraha and Hall, 2018), which has led to a narrowing of open sea between Asia and Australia and thereby facilitated overwater dispersal of Sundaic and/or Australo-Papuan lineages for many organismic groups (e.g. Heads, 2001; Irestedt et al., 2013; Gwee et al., 2017; Ng et al., 2017; Garg et al., 2018; Reilly et al., 2019; Oliver et al., 2020, including white-eyes).
evidence: This is supported by citations to geological studies.

claim: The narrowing of the sea gap between Asia and Australia has facilitated overwater dispersal of Sundaic and/or Australo-Papuan lineages for many organismic groups.
source: This is consistent with the rapid rate of tectonic change reconstructed for the Indonesian archipelago over the last 30 million years (Hall, 2002; Hall, 2012; de Bruyn et al., 2014; Nugraha and Hall, 2018), which has led to a narrowing of open sea between Asia and Australia and thereby facilitated overwater dispersal of Sundaic and/or Australo-Papuan lineages for many organismic groups (e.g. Heads, 2001; Irestedt et al., 2013; Gwee et al., 2017; Ng et al., 2017; Garg et al., 2018; Reilly et al., 2019; Oliver et al., 2020, including white-eyes).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple biogeographic studies.

claim: Most of the Wallacean region remains dominated by deep sea with no land bridges.
source: At the same time, while the narrowing of the sea gap between Australo-Papua and Asia has created numerous stepping-stone islands to facilitate overwater dispersal, most of the Wallacean region remains dominated by deep sea, and there are as yet no land bridges (Voris, 2000; Rheindt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Voris, 2000 and Rheindt et al., 2020.

claim: The complicated archipelagic setting has likely acted as a diversification driver in white-eyes.
source: This complicated archipelagic setting has likely acted as a diversification driver in white-eyes, which have the capability of colonizing and populating these deep-sea islands.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biogeographic patterns observed.

claim: Borneo and Java each harbor representatives of the Asiatic and Australasian clades.
source: To the west of Wallace's Line, the Sundaic islands of Borneo and Java, which constitute a large part of the Greater Sunda archipelago, each harbor a number of representatives of the Asiatic and Australasian clades but are additionally inhabited by the coastal endemic species Z. flavus.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Z. flavus is phylogenetically more closely related with the Indo-African clade than with the Asiatic and Australasian clades.
source: This species is phylogenetically more closely related with the Indo-African clade rather than with the geographically more proximate Asiatic and Australasian clades, demonstrating an impressive potential for dispersal capability that may in part underlie the rapid diversification rate of the genus.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Z. flavus demonstrates an impressive potential for dispersal capability.
source: This species is phylogenetically more closely related with the Indo-African clade rather than with the geographically more proximate Asiatic and Australasian clades, demonstrating an impressive potential for dispersal capability that may in part underlie the rapid diversification rate of the genus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic position and geographic distribution of Z. flavus.

claim: Low-lying Indonesian islands east of Wallace's Line generally harbor only Zosterops species from the Australasian clade.
source: Low-lying Indonesian islands to the east of Wallace's Line, such as Sumba and Kai, generally harbor only Zosterops species from the Australasian clade, whereas Z. japonicus of the Asiatic clade additionally occurs on islands that reach montane elevations of over 1200 m.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the distribution data in Figure 2a.

claim: Z. japonicus of the Asiatic clade additionally occurs on islands that reach montane elevations of over 1200 m.
source: Low-lying Indonesian islands to the east of Wallace's Line, such as Sumba and Kai, generally harbor only Zosterops species from the Australasian clade, whereas Z. japonicus of the Asiatic clade additionally occurs on islands that reach montane elevations of over 1200 m.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the distribution data.

claim: Z. japonicus is present on mountainous Buru but absent on Sumba.
source: For example, Z. japonicus is present on mountainous Buru (c. 9500 km2 in size) but absent on Sumba (c. 11,000 km2 in size), which largely comprises savannah with a small hilly region not exceeding 1200 m in elevation, despite Sumba being a larger island (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The elevation of an island contributes substantially to the number of main Zosterops clades present.
source: Although the elevation of an island contributes substantially to the number of main Zosterops clades present, it seems to have less influence on the total number of Zosterops species (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution patterns shown in Figure 1.

claim: Island elevation seems to have less influence on the total number of Zosterops species.
source: Although the elevation of an island contributes substantially to the number of main Zosterops clades present, it seems to have less influence on the total number of Zosterops species (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution patterns shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Kai islands harbor three distinct Zosterops species, including two island endemics Z. uropygialis and Z. grayi.
source: For instance, the Kai islands, with a combined area of only approximately 1400 km2 and an elevation of less than 700 m, harbor three distinct Zosterops species, including two island endemics Z. uropygialis and Z. grayi (not sampled) (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The widespread Lemon-bellied White-eye Z. chloris is non-monophyletic.
source: Our phylogenetic results reveal that the widespread Lemon-bellied White-eye Z. chloris is non-monophyletic (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and several small, low-lying islands situated between the Banda Sea and Arafura Sea, including Kai and Aru, may harbor a cryptic species morphologically identical to the Lemon-bellied White-eye.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several small islands between the Banda Sea and Arafura Sea may harbor a cryptic species morphologically identical to Z. chloris.
source: Our phylogenetic results reveal that the widespread Lemon-bellied White-eye Z. chloris is non-monophyletic (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and several small, low-lying islands situated between the Banda Sea and Arafura Sea, including Kai and Aru, may harbor a cryptic species morphologically identical to the Lemon-bellied White-eye.
evidence: This is an inference based on the non-monophyly of Z. chloris shown in Figure 2.

claim: White-eyes are renowned for their conservative morphology.
source: White-eyes are renowned for their conservative morphology, which contributes to the confusion that has surrounded their taxonomic treatment (Mees, 1957; Mayr, 1965; Lim et al., 2019; Manthey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple taxonomic studies.

claim: Borneo has been identified as a major source of diversification across Southeast Asia for various organismic groups.
source: Borneo has been identified as a major source of diversification across the Southeast Asian region for a variety of organismic groups, including birds, mammals, amphibians, and plants (de Bruyn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to de Bruyn et al., 2014.

claim: Borneo is the only place in the distribution of Zosterops where members of all three main clades occur.
source: Our study reveals Borneo's unique status as the only place in the distribution of the genus where members of all three main Zosterops clades occur, and where as many as four Zosterops species co-exist within a few square kilometers of one another, rendering it the center of faunal mixing for white-eyes (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: As many as four Zosterops species co-exist within a few square kilometers of one another on Borneo.
source: Our study reveals Borneo's unique status as the only place in the distribution of the genus where members of all three main Zosterops clades occur, and where as many as four Zosterops species co-exist within a few square kilometers of one another, rendering it the center of faunal mixing for white-eyes (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the distribution data.

claim: Borneo is the center of faunal mixing for white-eyes.
source: Our study reveals Borneo's unique status as the only place in the distribution of the genus where members of all three main Zosterops clades occur, and where as many as four Zosterops species co-exist within a few square kilometers of one another, rendering it the center of faunal mixing for white-eyes (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-occurrence of all three main clades on Borneo.

claim: For the longest time over the past 400,000 years, the Greater Sunda Islands and Malay Peninsula have been merged into Sundaland.
source: For the longest time over the past 400,000 years, however, these landmasses have been merged into a larger landmass, Sundaland, that has facilitated the evolution of much of Southeast Asia's equatorial rainforest fauna (Sarr et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sarr et al., 2019.

claim: Sundaland has facilitated the evolution of much of Southeast Asia's equatorial rainforest fauna.
source: For the longest time over the past 400,000 years, however, these landmasses have been merged into a larger landmass, Sundaland, that has facilitated the evolution of much of Southeast Asia's equatorial rainforest fauna (Sarr et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sarr et al., 2019.

claim: The east of Sundaland (Borneo) has constituted a particularly stable part of this subcontinent.
source: The east of Sundaland (i.e. Borneo) has constituted a particularly stable part of this subcontinent, remaining above water for the longest uninterrupted time and offering a wide variety of habitats such as mangroves (Z. flavus), submontane forest (Z. atricapilla and Z. auriventer), montane forest (Z. emiliae and a still undescribed white-eye from the Meratus range Eaton et al., 2016), and coastal woodland (Z. simplex).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by geological knowledge.

claim: Borneo has remained above water for the longest uninterrupted time.
source: The east of Sundaland (i.e. Borneo) has constituted a particularly stable part of this subcontinent, remaining above water for the longest uninterrupted time and offering a wide variety of habitats such as mangroves (Z. flavus), submontane forest (Z. atricapilla and Z. auriventer), montane forest (Z. emiliae and a still undescribed white-eye from the Meratus range Eaton et al., 2016), and coastal woodland (Z. simplex).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by geological knowledge.

claim: Ancestral range estimation suggests an Asian origin for the entire Zosterops radiation.
source: Our results from ancestral range estimation suggest an Asian origin for the entire Zosterops radiation, and a Sundaic origin for the Australasian clade (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ancestral range estimation suggests a Sundaic origin for the Australasian clade.
source: Our results from ancestral range estimation suggest an Asian origin for the entire Zosterops radiation, and a Sundaic origin for the Australasian clade (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Borneo constitutes the largest landmass within the Sundaic region.
source: Borneo constitutes the largest landmass within the Sundaic region, and its elevated count in discrete Zosterops lineages suggests that it has played a key role in the diversification of this important radiation.
evidence: This is a factual statement supported by geographic knowledge.

claim: Borneo's elevated count in discrete Zosterops lineages suggests it has played a key role in the diversification of this radiation.
source: Borneo constitutes the largest landmass within the Sundaic region, and its elevated count in discrete Zosterops lineages suggests that it has played a key role in the diversification of this important radiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic and biogeographic data.

claim: Borneo's exceptional biodiversity has been appreciated since Alfred R. Wallace's times.
source: While Borneo's exceptional biodiversity has been appreciated as early as during Alfred R. Wallace's times (Wallace, 1962), most of this diversity has traditionally been interpreted as being of a Sundaic element largely shared with Sumatra and peninsular Malaysia, and is only slowly being recognized as having attained species-level depths of differentiation (Cros et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wallace, 1962 and Cros et al., 2020.

claim: Borneo is known for hosting a number of deep phylogenetic isolates, such as the Bristlehead Pityriasis gymnocephala.
source: On the other hand, Borneo is known for hosting a number of deep phylogenetic isolates, such as the enigmatic Bristlehead Pityriasis gymnocephala (Oliveros et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oliveros et al., 2019.

claim: Z. emiliae has been shown to be embedded within Zosterops for over a decade.
source: Although it has been shown to be embedded within Zosterops for over a decade (Moyle et al., 2009; Cai et al., 2019), it continues to be treated as a monospecific genus (Chlorocharis) by some modern sources (del Hoyo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moyle et al., 2009 and Cai et al., 2019.

claim: Z. emiliae continues to be treated as a monospecific genus (Chlorocharis) by some modern sources.
source: Although it has been shown to be embedded within Zosterops for over a decade (Moyle et al., 2009; Cai et al., 2019), it continues to be treated as a monospecific genus (Chlorocharis) by some modern sources (del Hoyo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to del Hoyo et al., 2016.

claim: Z. emiliae emerged as a basal sister to the Australasian clade with moderate support.
source: Using our much-improved taxon sampling, Z. emiliae emerged as a basal sister to the Australasian clade with moderate support under various analytical regimes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cai et al., 2019 placed Z. emiliae with members of the Asiatic clade.
source: In contrast, Cai et al., 2019 placed Z. emiliae with members of the Asiatic clade.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings of Cai et al., 2019.

claim: ABBA-BABA tests did not identify an excess of allele sharing between Z. emiliae and the Asiatic members.
source: Our use of the ABBA-BABA test to verify whether this conflicting position may be due to ancient introgression did not identify an excess of allele sharing between Z. emiliae and the Asiatic members (set five in Table 1), suggesting that the incongruent placement of Z. emiliae by Cai et al., 2019 is unlikely to be a result of secondary gene flow.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Table 1.

claim: The incongruent placement of Z. emiliae by Cai et al., 2019 is unlikely to be a result of secondary gene flow.
source: Our use of the ABBA-BABA test to verify whether this conflicting position may be due to ancient introgression did not identify an excess of allele sharing between Z. emiliae and the Asiatic members (set five in Table 1), suggesting that the incongruent placement of Z. emiliae by Cai et al., 2019 is unlikely to be a result of secondary gene flow.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ABBA-BABA test results shown in Table 1.

claim: Incomplete lineage sorting may have generated phylogenetic conflict in the placement of Z. emiliae.
source: Instead, incomplete lineage sorting may have generated such phylogenetic conflict as the divergence of Z. emiliae likely fell within a time of rapid diversification within the genus, leading to its recalcitrance to phylogenetic resolution when only few loci are applied.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the conflicting placement of Z. emiliae.

claim: The identification of areas in western Indonesia as a major center of modern phylogenetic diversity elevates their status as a region of global conservation relevance.
source: The identification of areas in western Indonesia as a major center of modern phylogenetic diversity not only contributes to their recognition as an arena of important evolutionary processes, but also elevates their status as a region of global conservation relevance.
evidence: This is an inference about the conservation implications of the study's findings.

claim: A total of 48 historical toepad samples and 52 fresh samples were acquired.
source: A total of 48 historical toepad samples and 52 fresh samples were acquired from various museums and through fieldwork conducted across peninsular Malaysia and the Indonesian archipelago (Ashari et al., 2019; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The study designed 832 loci targeting both conserved exons and variable intronic regions.
source: We designed loci specifically targeting both conserved exons and variable intronic regions of the Zosterops genome (Chattopadhyay et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: A total of 63,244 RNA baits were designed by Arbor Biosciences.
source: After filtering, our design retained 832 loci, which were used by Arbor Biosciences (USA) to design a total of 63,244 RNA baits.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Each locus was targeted with 4X tiling density of overlapping baits.
source: Each locus was targeted with 4X tiling density of overlapping baits, each bait of 100 bp, for in-solution target enrichment.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: 770 loci were retained after visual quality checks.
source: We removed four historical samples due to high amount of missing data and kept 770 loci after visual quality checks across all samples, ensuring each locus is present in at least 85% of individuals and contains less than 30% missing nucleotides.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The final concatenated alignment was 1,635,155 bp with 7.60% gaps.
source: All 770 loci were concatenated, giving a final alignment of 1,635,155 bp with 7.60% gaps.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: 768 gene trees were rooted with M. gularis for species tree inference.
source: A total of 768 gene trees were rooted with M. gularis, while no outgroup sequence was present for two gene trees which had to be discarded for species tree inference.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Nodes with less than 68% bootstrap support were collapsed.
source: Nodes with less than 68% bootstrap support were collapsed.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The study expanded clade assignment to 30 Zosterops taxa not sampled but found to be embedded within one of the three main clades with high bootstrap support by previous studies.
source: We expanded our clade assignment to 30 Zosterops taxa not sampled in our study but found to be embedded within one of the three main clades with high bootstrap support (>90%) by at least one study up until 2019 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Non-specific binding during hybridization allowed assembly of mitochondrial DNA from raw reads.
source: We observed non-specific binding during hybridization of probes and sample DNA, allowing us to assemble mitochondrial DNA from the raw reads of each individual prepared by target capture.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: 1041 bp of ND2 sequence was extracted from each individual.
source: Finally, we extracted 1041 bp of ND2 sequence from each individual by aligning each assembled mitogenome to the ND2 sequence of Z. lateralis.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: ND2 sequences of 68 individuals were retained for phylogenetic analysis.
source: Some samples were removed due to extensive missing nucleotides, and the ND2 sequences of 68 individuals were retained.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: A positive critical value Z > 3 in ABBA-BABA tests suggests a significant excess of ABBA-like alleles compared to BABA-like alleles.
source: A positive critical value Z > 3, corresponding to a p-value below 0.0013, suggests a significant excess of ABBA-like alleles as compared to BABA-like alleles (Green et al., 2010; Patterson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section and supported by citations.

claim: PHRAPL simulations were conducted on four combinations of populations with 770 gene trees.
source: We conducted simulations on a smaller subset of populations exhibiting topological incongruence: Z. auriventer (A), Z. atricapilla (B), Z. simplex (C), Z. emiliae (D) and Z. melanurus (E). A total of four combinations (ACD, ACE, BCD and BCE) were tested with 770 gene trees, each dataset consisting of three populations and an outgroup, Z. senegalensis.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: 48 possible demographic models were generated under specific settings in PHRAPL.
source: We generated 48 possible demographic models under the following settings: an overall maximum of three free parameters (K = 3), a maximum of two coalescent events (K = 2), either complete isolation or migration event(s) with a single rate (K = 1), no variation in population size and growth (K = 1), only fully resolved trees were assumed, and only symmetrical migration between populations was assumed.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: BioGeoBEARS was run to estimate the ancestral range of each internal node.
source: We ran BioGeoBEARS 1.1.2 (Matzke, 2014) in R 3.6.1 (R Development Core Team, 2019) to estimate the ancestral range of each internal node of the unrooted ML concatenated tree.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: Each species was assigned to one or more out of ten geographical areas for ancestral range estimation.
source: We assigned each species to one or more out of ten geographical areas: the Afrotropical region, West Indian Ocean islands, South Asia, mainland Southeast Asia, East Asia, Philippines, the Sundaic region, Wallacea, Melanesia, and Australia.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.

claim: The best-fitting model for ancestral range estimation was DEC+j based on AIC values.
source: We applied all six models (DEC, DEC+j, DIVA, DIVA+j, BayArea and BayArea+j) and selected the best-fitting model (DEC+j) based on AIC values.
evidence: This is stated in the materials and methods section.
